tecnicas.observacao: Pacote de prompting de um passo: instrução de papel no sistema («As an debugger, you should refine the buggy program for bug report») → instrucao; exemplo fixo único (bug report e função refinada) → exemplos, que também restringe o formato de saída a uma função refinada completa → restricoes; bug report com código da função defeituosa, documentação/comentários, entradas e saídas esperadas dos testes falhos e mensagens de erro → contexto; 10 amostras por bug validadas por testes e depois manualmente → amostragem. Não há iteração guiada por erros sobre a saída gerada (as mensagens de erro são do programa original, insumo de contexto), por isso não recebe feedback. mecanismos_acrescentados em relação à condição Mask-Hunk (formato de entrada e saída do APR por preenchimento no mesmo arcabouço, Tabela IV): artefatos no lugar do trecho mascarado (contexto) e saída de função completa no lugar do trecho (restricoes); as duas categorias já estavam presentes na base com outro conteúdo. Contrafactual de pacote: Report-Func vs Mask-Hunk no DebugBench (mesmo modelo, 10 amostras), o que não autoriza atribuir o ganho a um único ingrediente. Na comparação com os sistemas da Tabela II (RQ1) os valores dos comparadores foram reaproveitados dos artigos originais, com outro orçamento de amostras e localização perfeita de trechos.

observacoes.descricao: O estudo declara não ter o objetivo de propor o D4C como nova técnica de APR, e sim um novo modo de usar LLMs em APR; o D4C é ainda assim o objeto de investigação.
Pressuposto de localização perfeita em nível de função: a função defeituosa é fornecida e o D4C escolhe as linhas a modificar; no cenário real, uma ferramenta de FL em nível de método a forneceria.

citacoes.trecho: In this paper, we investigate a new approach to adapt LLMs to program repair.
Based on this insight, we designed D4C, a straightforward prompting framework for APR.
To align LLM’s inference objective with its pre-trained completion objective, we adopt a one-shot prompting strategy.

As shown in Fig. 4, once the buggy function is identified, D4C will automated extract (1) documents or comments that describe the general purpose of the function and its input-output data types, (2) the inputs and expected outputs of the failed test cases, and (3) error messages from executing those failed test cases.

Following this, D4C integrates the bug report into a complete prompt, which is carefully designed to include a concise role-play system instruction (e.g., You are an AI debugger ...) and a fixed example consisting of a handcrafted bug report and its refined program.
This one-shot ICL also allows us to restrict the output format of the LLM to a refined function rather than other common output formats related to APR (e.g., unit diff patch [67]).
Furthermore, we adopt a much smaller sampling number of 10, as the inference budgets (fee, time, etc.) for LLMs are much larger than traditional methods.
To control a moderated randomness of text generation, we follow the previous work and set the randomness hyper-parameter, temperature, as 1.0.
In our implementation, we also carefully modified the system instructions to adapt to each output setting.

For the generated patches by Report-Hunk, as we do not provide a specific location to modify and cannot precisely determine where the generated patch should be applied, we instruct Mixtral-MoE to help us to automatically apply the generated patches to the original buggy program before patch validation.
w/o Document: D4C without including the program documents or function comments in the prompt.
w/o Test: D4C without including inputs and expected outputs of the failed test cases in the prompt.
w/o Message: D4C without including error message from the failed tests in the prompt.
- Pure: D4C without including any guidance like mask or artifacts to identify bugs in the prompt, i.e., an aligned LLM.
Since some of the baselines are not open-sourced, we cannot re-run them to reproduce the result.
Specifically, for baselines, the perfect buggy hunks within the buggy function is provided, while for D4C, only the buggy function is provided.
Since it contains data from previous versions of open-source projects where most code models have been trained on, it faces the threat of data leakage.
Since DebugBench is not exposed to the threat of data leakage, we use it for our insight validation (RQ2).
Table V shows that D4C generates a total of 210 plausible patches but 30 are incorrect with respect to the human patches.
To mitigate the potential bias in the manual analysis, two authors independently confirm the patch correctness.
Moreover, as LLM’s inference overhead and time cost is much higher than traditional APR tools, using LLM to generate patches for all given hunks may result in huge resource waste.
Given OpenAI’s pricing of $0.01 per 1,000 input tokens and $0.03 per 1,000 output tokens [76], the average cost per patch is $0.023 ($0.021 for resolved bugs and $0.024 for unresolved bugs).
Generating 10 patches per bug results in a total cost of $0.23 for the entire dataset.
Thus, there is a labor cost of manually validating the correctness of plausible patches beyond the token cost of patch generation.

As the effectiveness of the model may vary in different settings, our results may not generalize beyond the studied settings and other programming languages beyond the supported ones in Defects4J and DebugBench.
We mitigate this threat by reusing configurations in prior work, and widely used benchmarks.
Therefore, we decide to release our experimental results for public verification.

Thus, D4C can subsequently verify all 10 patches without involving significant waste of effort on incorrect patches (within 5 minutes), rather than suffering from a time-consuming process of verifying hundreds of patches (up to 5 hours [18], [25], [26], [30], [70]).
However, D4C requires running tests only up to 10 minutes per bug, with a timeout of 1min per patch.

This is because D4C only needs to generate at most 10 patches during decoding (i.e., beam search), which is significantly less than the sampling number of existing methods (i.e., over hundreds of sampling).
For Defects4J, the average input prompt length is 1,386.84 tokens overall, with 1,325.68 for resolved bugs and 1,369.72 for unresolved bugs.
In terms of sample size, we notice that a sample size of 10 is the optimal setting to allow D4C to find the correct patches.
Despite this, GPT-4 with the completion objective still fixes more bugs (414 vs 408) on DebugBench than GPT-4 with the infilling objective and masked hunk (“Mask-Hunk” in Table IV).
This paper is not aimed at proposing D4C as a new APR technique, but rather to introduce a new mindset or paradigm for better harnessing LLMs in APR in the future.
